extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent applicants/practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examiners (and practitioners) on evaluating whether claim language satisfies the definiteness requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre‑AIA 112 second paragraph), including claim construction, evidentiary standards, and procedures for making and resolving indefiniteness rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (35 U.S.C. 112(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph) requires that a patent application specification conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor regards as the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary purpose: ensure the scope of the claims is clear so the public is informed of the boundaries of infringement. Secondary purpose: provide a clear measure of what the inventor regards as the invention for evaluating patentability and whether the specification meets 35 U.S.C. 112(a). Claims that do not meet this standard must be rejected as indefinite; such rejections require the applicant to explain why the language is definite or amend the claim. Rejections must clearly identify the language that causes indefiniteness and thoroughly explain the reasoning for the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give claims their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) consistent with the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination a claim must be given its broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI reduces the chance an issued claim will be interpreted more broadly than justified; focus is what is reasonable from the perspective of one of ordinary skill. Plain meaning is used unless inconsistent with the specification. Sources for meaning include claim words, specification, drawings, and prior art, but the specification is the best source. Applicant may be their own lexicographer if a special meaning is clearly set forth in the specification. See cited Federal Circuit precedent (Yamamoto, Zletz, Buszard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain meaning of claim terms (ordinary and customary meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words of the claim must be given their plain meaning — the ordinary and customary meaning given by those of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention — unless inconsistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary use may be evidenced by the claims, specification, drawings, and prior art. The specification serving as a glossary gives greatest clarity. A presumption of plain meaning may be rebutted by a clear and intentional special definition in the specification as filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants are their own lexicographers but cannot add definitions after filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may define terms in the specification and thereby assign special meanings; however, an applicant may not add a special definition or disavowal after the filing date of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an Office action used plain meaning, applicant may point to where the specification as filed provides a special definition or disavowal. Any special definition relied on must be present in the specification as filed; adding new definitions during prosecution is not permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether each claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre‑AIA 112 sixth paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should determine whether each limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means‑plus‑function) or pre‑AIA sixth paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a limitation invokes 112(f)/sixth paragraph, the limitation must be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof. See MPEP § 2181 and In re Donaldson and related authorities for more on means/step‑plus‑function analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness standard: skilled artisan must understand what is claimed in light of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: A decision on indefiniteness requires determining whether those skilled in the art would understand what is claimed when the claim is read in light of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During prosecution, applicants have the opportunity and duty to amend ambiguous claims. If, under BRI and in view of the specification, a person of ordinary skill would read a claim with more than one reasonable interpretation, the claim is indefinite and should be rejected. Examiners should analyze claim terms from the perspective of those skilled in the relevant art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims during examination are construed differently than issued claims in court
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office construes claims during examination by applying the BRI consistent with the specification; courts construe patented claims differently, using the prosecution record and without BRI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patented claims in court are not given BRI and must inform those skilled in the art of scope with reasonable certainty (Nautilus). The PTO applies a lower threshold for ambiguity during prosecution because claims can be amended to sharpen clarity; this may result in a lower threshold for indefiniteness than in court. Examiners should therefore apply BRI to identify ambiguities that can be corrected during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold requirements of clarity and precision
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner’s focus is whether the claim meets the threshold requirements of clarity and precision set forth in the statute, not whether more suitable language is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must set out and circumscribe a particular subject matter with a reasonable degree of clarity and particularity. The essential inquiry looks to: (A) content of the application disclosure; (B) teachings of prior art; and (C) claim interpretation by one of ordinary skill in the pertinent art. Allow some latitude in manner of expression so long as 112(b) is satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claim as a whole and interaction of limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: In reviewing claims for compliance with 112(b), the examiner must consider the claim as a whole to determine whether it apprises one of ordinary skill in the art of its scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The totality of limitations and their interactions must be considered to ascertain the inventor’s contribution and whether the claim serves its notice function (see Larsen). Do not read limitations into claims from preferred embodiments absent a clear disclaimer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth is not indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad claim is not indefinite merely because it encompasses a wide scope, provided the scope is clearly defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a genus claim covering multiple species is broad but not indefinite if it is clear which species are covered. A claim is indefinite when it could be interpreted in a way that makes it unclear which species are included (e.g., more than one reasonable interpretation). See MPEP § 2173.05(h) and Markush discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners must establish a clear record when making an indefiniteness rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: When an examiner determines a term or phrase is prima facie indefinite, the examiner should clearly communicate findings and reasons supporting the rejection to create a complete prosecution record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office action should set forth the specific term or phrase that is indefinite and why the metes and bounds are unclear; avoid mere conclusions. Provide detailed explanation and, whenever practicable, indicate how the issues may be resolved to overcome the rejection. See MPEP § 706.03, § 707.07(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action must provide sufficient explanation to permit a meaningful applicant response
rubrics_metrics.description: Because an indefiniteness rejection requires applicant to explain why the language is not indefinite or to amend the claim, the Office action should provide enough information for the applicant to prepare a meaningful response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out the specific term or phrase, explain in detail why it renders the metes and bounds unclear, and, when practicable, indicate how the indefiniteness issues may be resolved. Failure to adequately respond to a prima facie case may allow the examiner to make the rejection final. See MPEP § 707.07(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners encouraged to suggest claim language but not insist on preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may suggest claim language to improve clarity or precision, but should not insist on examiner’s own linguistic preferences if applicant's language satisfies statutory requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow latitude in the manner of expression so long as 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is satisfied. Suggest improvements but do not force a particular phrasing when alternate phrasing meets the requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants may resolve indefiniteness by amending claims or providing persuasive explanation/evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: In response to an indefiniteness rejection, the applicant may amend the claim or provide a persuasive explanation (with evidence as necessary) that a person of ordinary skill would not consider the language unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some cases the applicant may need to provide a separate definition (e.g., art‑recognized dictionary) to show how the ordinarily‑skilled artisan would understand the claim language. If the examiner is persuaded, the examiner should indicate the previous rejection is withdrawn and explain what prompted the change (referencing applicant’s remarks where appropriate) to clarify the prosecution record.

rubrics_metrics.name: No per se rules; indefiniteness examples are fact specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Office policy is not to employ per se rules to make technical rejections for indefiniteness; examples set forth in MPEP are fact specific and should not be applied as per se rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP § 2173.05 lists numerous rationales that may support an indefiniteness rejection (e.g., functional claim limitations, relative terminology/terms of degree, lack of antecedent basis). Use the facts of the case to support the rejection; do not adopt blanket categorical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: When more information is necessary, consider a requirement for information under 37 CFR 1.105
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner determines more information is necessary to ascertain the meaning of a claim term, a requirement for information under 37 CFR 1.105 may be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 704.10 regarding requirements for information. Use procedural tools when needed to clarify claim meaning rather than defaulting to a rejection without giving applicant opportunity to supply information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness arises if claim, under BRI, has more than one reasonable interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the language of a claim, given its broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification, is such that a person of ordinary skill in the relevant art would read it with more than one reasonable interpretation, then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should distinguish between breadth (acceptable) and ambiguity (not acceptable). Provide a clear rationale showing the multiple reasonable interpretations and why that creates uncertainty about the metes and bounds of the claimed subject matter.
